text:
Verses 5–16

This section of verses recounts the words and deeds of the idolaters in response to the Prophet’s claim of receiving divine revelation and to the verses of the Qurʾan that were sent down to him, before responding to them with conclusive arguments.

For example, it mentions how they belittled God by asking, ‘What is keeping the punishment back from us?’ Or ‘why has no treasure been sent down to him?’, ‘Why has no angel been sent with him?’ and claiming, ‘He has fabricated the Qurʾan!’ These verses contain other insights

besides these as well.

(11:5) Look! They fold up (yathnūn) their breasts to hide from him (li-yastakhfū min-hu). Look! W hen they draw their cloaks over their heads, He knows whatever they keep secret and whatever they disclose. Indeed He knows best whatever is in the breasts.

The verb thanā (yathnūn, ‘fold up’) means to bend something back onto itself. In M ajmaʿ al-bayān, al-Ṭabrisī writes:

‘The original meaning of thanā is ‘to attach’ (ʿaṭf). From this is derived the word ithnān (‘two’), because you have two of a thing when you join one to another; from this is also derived thanāʾ (‘praise’) because when you praise someone you attach positive qualities to them; from this is also derived istithnāʾ (‘exception’), because it means to attach one thing to another by removing it from it.’ He also says, ‘Istikhfāʾ (‘to hide’) means to try to conceal something. The same is true of istighshāʾ (‘to cover’).’

So when God says, They fold up their breasts to hide from it, this means that they turn their chests backwards and lower their heads to hide from the Book, meaning to keep themselves from hearing it when it is being recited. In reality, this means that they are trying to hide from the Prophet and avoid being in his presence when he is reciting the Qurʾan to them to convey its message, so that they do not have to respond to his arguments. Look! W hen they draw their cloaks over their heads, He knows whatever they keep secret and whatever they disclose: This suggests that they

used to cover their heads with their garments when hiding by folding their chests. God mentions this and informs them that He knows whatever they conceal and whatever they reveal at that time, so hiding does not avail them from listening to the Qurʾan and God knows them in their private and public lives.

Some commentators have said that what is meant by their wrapping themselves in their garments is their covering themselves in their homes at night when they lie in their beds to sleep, which is the most hidden and private state a person can be in. In this case, the meaning of the verse is: ‘They fold up their chests to hide from this Book when it is recited to them, but God knows them in private and in public and even in the most hidden state they can be in, which is when they cover themselves with their garments for sleep.’ And this reading of the verse is not without merit. This is what the context implies about the meaning of the verse, and other meanings that do not match the context have also been proposed for it. For example, some have said that the pronoun ‘it’ in They fold up their breasts to hide from it refers back to God, or to the Prophet. Others have said that they fold up their breasts means ‘they fold up their hearts in disbelief.’ Still others have said it means ‘they fold up their hearts in enmity to the Prophet.’ However, these are all far-fetched meanings for the verse.

(11:6) There is no animal (dābba) on the earth, but that its sustenance lies with Allah, and He knows its abode and its temporary

place of lodging. Everything is in a manifest Book.

According to the Arabic lexicons, the term dābba (‘animal’) generally refers to anything that moves. However, the term is often used to refer to specific types of creatures. The context of the verse necessitates a more general interpretation, as the discourse is intended to demonstrate the vastness of God’s knowledge, as it follows on from His saying in the previous

verse: W hen they draw their cloaks over their heads, He knows whatever they keep secret and whatever they disclose. Indeed He knows best whatever is in the breasts (11:5).

This explanation, namely that God must provide for each and every creature, is intended to demonstrate the breadth of His knowledge, that encompasses each and every creature in all of its states of being. This, in turn, suggests that the phrase, He knows its abode and its temporary place of lodging is, in essence, an explanatory clause for His saying, its sustenance lies with Allah. Therefore, the meaning is that every creature on earth relies on God for sustenance, and they would not exist without it. God, the Exalted, knows and is aware of each creature’s condition, wherever it may be. If it resides in a fixed abode, like a whale in the water or a shellfish embedded in the earth, its provision is there. If it leaves its dwelling place and has a temporary place of lodging from which it will eventually return to the former, like a bird in the air, a traveller away from home, or an embryo in the womb, its provision is there. In summary, He, the Exalted, is aware of the condition of each and every creature on earth. And how could He not be, when He is responsible for their provision? The sustenance only reaches the recipient with the knowledge of the Provider of this sustenance about the recipient and His knowledge of the recipient’s permanent or temporary, stationary or transitory place of residence.

From this, it appears that what is meant by ‘abode’ (mustaqarr) and ‘temporary place of lodging’ (mustawdaʿ) is the place where the creature settles as long as it is a moving being on earth, living a worldly life, and the place where it dwells, then leaves, and departs from. However, what some interpreters have said is that what is meant by abode and mustaqarr are its places during its life and after its death, or that they refer to loins and wombs, or that they refer to its homes on earth when they actually exist and their existence as raw materials when they were only potentially existent. However, all of these meanings are far removed from the context of the verse, except if His saying, and He knows its abode and its temporary place of lodging, is considered an independent statement in its own right and not an explanation of what precedes it.

Interested readers can refer to our commentary on the verse, It is He who created you from a single soul, then there is the (enduring) abode and the place of temporary lodging (6:98), which will shed further light on the meaning of the verse under discussion here.

As for His saying, … but that its sustenance lies with Allah …, this indicates that God is responsible for providing for His creatures. It is repeatedly many times in the Qurʾan that provision (rizq) is the sole purview of

God and that it is something that the creatures can expect from Him. For example, He says: W ho is it that may provide for you if He withholds His provision? (67:21); Indeed it is Allah who is the All-provider, Powerful, Allstrong (51:58); And in the sky is your provision and what you are promised.

By the Lord of the sky and the earth, it is indeed the truth, just as you speak

(51:22–23).

There is no problem in affirming that there is something due from God to others, since He is the one who has bound Himself to that obligation without anyone else’s intervention. There are many such parallels for

this in the Qurʾan. For example, He says: He has made mercy incumbent upon Himself (6:12); … and it was a must for Us to help the faithful (30:47). Rational contemplation supports this view, because sustenance is what maintains the existence of a living creature, and since its existence emanates from the bounty of His generosity, what it relies on for sustenance is from Him as well. And, since there is no partner with Him in creating it, there can be no partner with Him in what its existence depends on, meaning its sustenance (rizq).

We have already discussed the meaning of the phrase ‘manifest Book’ (kitāb mubīn) in our commentary on verses 6:59 and 10:61, so let readers refer there.1

(11:7) It is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days— and His Throne was upon the waters—that He may test you:

which of you is best in conduct. Yet if you say, ‘You will indeed be raised up after death,’ the faithless will surely say, ‘This is nothing but plain magic.’

1 See al-Mīzān Eng. v. 13 (Ed.)

We will present the full account of the creation of the heavens and the earth based on the apparent meaning of the Qurʾan and the explanations of the Infallibles in our commentary on Sūrah Fuṣṣilat.

In short, the apparent meaning of the phrase, in six days, and the phrase, and His Throne was upon the waters, is that God’s description of the creation of the heavens (samāwāt—note that this word is plural) along with the earth in six days refers to the layers of the visible material creation that exist above our earth, as whatever is above something and overshadows it is a samāʾ for it—this is what scholars have said. And the concepts of ‘above’ and ‘below’ are always in relation to something else.

These are layers of the material creation that exist above our earth and envelop it. The earth is spherical in shape as suggested by His saying, Exalted is He: “He draws the night’s cover over the day, which pursues it swiftly (7:54).

The first heaven (samāʾ) is the one adorned by the lamps of stars and planets; it is the layer that contains them or it is above them and is adorned by them, like a ceiling is adorned with lanterns and chandeliers. As for what is above this nearest heaven, there is nothing in His speech describing its characteristics other than what is in His saying, He created seven heavens in layers (67:3), and His saying, Have you not seen how Allah has created seven heavens in layers, and has made therein the moon for a light, and the sun for a lamp (71:16). This indicates that they are stacked one above the other. In His description of their creation, God has said that these heavens were initially interwoven, and then He split them apart. They became scattered and disintegrated, then He gathered and stacked them. They were

initially smoke, and He made them into heavens. See the verses: Have the faithless not regarded that the heavens and the earth were interwoven and We unravelled them, and We made every living thing out of water? Will they not then have faith? (21:30) Then He turned to the heaven, and it was smoke, and He said to it and to the earth, ‘Come! W illingly or unwillingly!’ They said, ‘We come heartily.’ Then He set them up as seven heavens in two days, and revealed in each heaven its ordinance (41:11–12).

This indicates that the creation of the heavens was completed in two of the six days of creation. Now, the term ‘day’ (yawm) denotes a measurable unit of time, and it is not necessary for a ‘day’ in all circumstances and contexts to correspond to a day on earth, which is derived from one rotation

of its axial motion. For example, one lunar day, as related to this Earth, is equivalent to approximately twenty-nine and a half days on Earth. The use of the term ‘day’ to denote a period of time is common in discourse. Therefore, what this means is that God created the seven heavens in two periods of time. Similarly, about the Earth, He has said that He created the earth in two days… and ordained therein its means of sustenance

in four days (41:9-10). Therefore, in this verse, He tells us that the earth was created in two days, which are epochs or stages, and that He set up its sustenance in four days, which refers to the four seasons.

The conclusions we draw from these verses is, firstly, that the creation of the heavens and the earth as we see them today in their form and shape was not from absolute nothingness. Instead, they previously existed as an undifierentiated, compound, mass of material. Some parts of this matter were separated from others and made into the earth in two periods of time. The sky was initially smoke, which was separated and arranged into seven heavens, also within two periods of time.

Secondly, whatever living things we perceive are made from water.

Therefore, water is the substance of life.

Given what we have explained, the meaning of the verse presently under discussion becomes clear. When He said, It is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days, the intended meaning of their creation is the gathering of their components, their division, and their splitting from whatever else was mixed with them from this undifierentiated matter. The original creation and fusion in the heavens and the earth were completed in two days each, leaving two remaining days of the six for the remainder of the creation.

As for when God says, and His Throne was upon the waters, this is an adverbial statement, meaning that, on the day of the creations of the heavens, His Throne was upon the waters. The fact that the Throne was upon

the waters on that day is a metaphor for His Exalted Sovereignty being established upon this water, which is the substance of life. Therefore, the Throne of God is a symbol of His Sovereignty. Its establishment upon a location signifies the establishment of His Sovereignty over it. Similarly, His being upon the Throne implies encompassing Sovereignty and its management.

As for those who say that the intended meaning of the Throne (ʿarsh) is a structure, they derive this meaning from the verse, and the trellises that they erect (16:68). However, this explanation does not make sense here. ... that He may test you (li-yabluwa-kum): which of you is best in conduct: The lām in li-yabluwa-kum is purposive. To test someone is to submit them to examination or trial. The phrase, which of you is best in conduct, expounds the nature of this test in the form of a question, meaning that He created the heavens and the earth in the form that He did for

the purpose of testing you and distinguishing those who do good from those who do bad.

It is known that a test or trial is an action carried out for a purpose other than itself, namely to distinguish good from bad, virtuous from vicious, righteous from wicked. Equally, it is only necessary to distinguish good from bad because of the consequences they bear in terms of reward or punishment. Likewise, divine recompense is intended to fulfil God’s true promise. That is why we find Him mentioning each of these consequential matters as a purpose of creation. For example, regarding trials

being the purpose of creation, He says: Indeed We have made whatever is on the earth an adornment for it that We may test them: which of them is best in conduct? (18:7);

Regarding the discernment and distinction, He has said: … so that Allah may separate the bad ones from the good (8:37);

While on the subject of divine recompense, He says: Allah created the heavens and the earth with reason, so that every soul may be requited for what it has earned, and they will not be wronged (45:22);

Concerning the fulfilment of His promise, He says: We will bring it back as We began the first creation—a promise binding on Us. That indeed We will do (21:105).

And other such verses. He says regarding worship being the purpose in the creation of the jinn and humans, I did not create the jinn and the humans except that they may worship Me (51:56).

Now, considering righteous deeds or the virtuous human as the purpose of creation does not contradict the fact that creation encompasses

other purposes as well. After all, man is truly one of those purposes. This is because the unity and connectivity governing the world allows for each type of being to be considered a purpose of creation. Since it is the result of the connection and the outcome of the general association between its constituent parts, it is possible to speak about each type of creation as the intended objective of the creation of the heavens and the earth, since the creation of these leads to its existence.

However, the human being is the most perfect and well-crafted of the material creations contained in the heavens and the earth. If he fiourishes in terms of his knowledge and good deeds, he becomes the best and the highest in status and degree compared to all other creatures. Some creations, like

the heavens, have been given a more powerful creation than him, as God has said. It is evident that the perfection of creation is its intended purpose when it includes the imperfect. Therefore, we consider the different stages of human existence from sperm, to fetus, to childhood, among others, as precursors to the existence of a healthy, fiourishing human being, and so on. Based on this, it becomes clear that the best individuals among humans, if there are those who are absolutely the best, are the true purpose behind the creation of the heavens and the earth. The wording of the verse also indicates this. For example, when He says, which of you is best in conduct, this implies that the aim is to distinguish who is best in deed from all others, regardless of whether they are virtuous or wicked. Thus, whoever’s

deeds are better than the rest, whether the rest are virtuous and their deeds are merely inferior to his, or whether they are wicked, the distinguishing of the one who is best in deeds from all others is the intended purpose of creation. Therefore, this explains the significance of the ḥadīth qudsī, in which God addresses His Prophet, saying, ‘Were it not for you, I would not have created the firmament’ (law lā-ka lammā khalaqtu al-aflāk)—this is because he is the best of all creation.

In M ajmaʿ al-Bayān, we read: ‘Al-Jubāʾī said: “The verse indicates that he existed before the creation of the heavens, the earth, and the angels. This is because there is no point in creating the throne upon the waters unless it provides some benefit to a morally accountable being capable of inferring from it, so there must be a living, morally accountable being at that

time.” ʿAlī b. ʿĪsā, however, said: “There is nothing to say that informing the Qurʾan’s audience of the creation of the throne upon the waters would not benefit morally accountable beings and, thus, there is no need for what al-Jubāʾī has said.” This was the preferred view of Sayyid al-M urtaḍā.’ Author’s comment: Their assertions are based on the Muʿtazilī doctrine that God’s actions follow a purpose and aimed at producing good

and beneficial results, even if that involves creating things to inform morally accountable beings about them, so that they may contemplate and

believe in Him, hence accomplishing a benefit for them. In our previous discussions, we have already established that God Almighty is not governed by anything, nor is He influenced by anything other than Himself,

be it a benefit or any other supposed concept, and that everything other than Him is created by Him and subject to His command, even if it is an objective existent reality. The decision belongs only to God, and God is the Creator of everything.

These aspects of goodness and benefit—which are what motivate us to act— exist in objective reality and afiect us insofar as we are active agents in pursuit of a happy life. God, however, is far superior to that. These aspects of goodness and benefits are general rules derived from the cosmic order and the relations that exist between created entities. It is crucial to acknowledge that the universe and the order within it are His creation. It is quite impossible for a derived concept to precede the action from which it is derived then go beyond it and even surpass the agent who originated it. As for the rationale given for the creation of the heavens and the earth in the verse, that He may test you: which of you is best in conduct, and its many parallels in the Qurʾan, they are rationales that are based on the benefits and advantages that derive from an action. God has informed us that

His actions are never devoid of goodness, as He described Himself as the one who perfected everything that He created (32:7). God is the epitome of goodness; there is no evil in Him, and there is no ugliness with Him. Therefore, nothing evil or ugly ever originates from Him.

The preceding discussion does not necessitate that the meaning of ‘good’ is ‘whatever emanates from God’ or ‘whatever He has commanded, even if reason finds it repugnant’, nor that ‘evil’ is ‘whatever does not emanate from Him’ or ‘whatever He has prohibited, even if reason finds it to

be good and just.’ This claim is rejected by verses such as “Indeed Allah does not enjoin indecencies (7:28).

Yet if you say, ‘You will indeed be raised up after death,’ the faithless will surely say, ‘This is nothing but plain magic’: Insofar as the previous statement, that He may test you, points to the Resurrection, this passage calls attention to the disbelievers’ response to the Prophet’s mention of the afterlife by accusing him of being a magician of speech.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that they, just as they dismissed the eloquence and rhetoric of the Qurʾan as magic, so too did they dismiss as magic the realities conveyed by the Qurʾan and the Prophet which their minds refused to accept, such as the teaching of resurrection after death. Therefore, this represents the extent to which they were willing to lie about the Qurʾan and the depths of their obstinacy and defiance towards truth, as they went beyond labelling its eloquent language as magic, to actually dismissing its truthful ideas as magic.

It is important to consider that ‘magic’ (siḥr) here might not mean literal magic in the sense of sorcery, but in the figurative sense of deception

and obfuscation by presenting falsehood in the guise of truth. However, this reading does not align with the apparent meaning of God’s words in a similar context: Say, ‘In whose hand is the dominion of all things, and who shelters and no shelter can be provided from Him, if you know?’ They will say, ‘to Allah.’ Say, ‘Then how are you being deluded?’ (23:89).

(11:8) And, surely, if We defer their punishment until a certain time, they will surely say, ‘W hat holds it back?’ Look! On the day it overtakes them it shall not be turned away from them, and they will be besieged by what they used to deride.

Note the use of particles of emphasis at the beginning of the verse. The meaning is: ‘I swear that if we delay the punishment these disbelievers deserve, they would mockingly say, “What is holding back this promised punishment from us, and why has it not descended upon us or afflicted us?”’

This shows that what they heard from God’s speech or the Prophet’s speech a threat of inescapable punishment, and if God delays this punishment as a mercy for them, they deride it and mock it, by asking, ‘What

holds it back?’ This is supported by the following statement, Look! On the day it overtakes them it shall not be turned away from them, and they will be besieged by what they used to deride.

This supports the idea that Sūrah Hūd was revealed after Sūrah Yūnus, on account of the content of the latter, beginning with the verse, There is a messenger for every nation; so when their messenger comes, judgment is made between them with justice, and they are not wronged.

In the phrase, until a certain time (ilā umma maʿdūda), the term umma means ‘time’ (and not ‘nation’), as per the verse, Said the one of the two who had been delivered, remembering after a long time (baʿd umma) (12:45). Alternatively, umma could be used here in the sense of a group of people (meaning then, ‘for the sake of a specified nation’). God has promised

to support this religion with a group of righteous people who would not allow anything to impair their faith. And when this happens, the believers will be able to follow the religion which God has approved for them.

In this regard, He has said, Allah will soon bring a people whom He loves and who love Him, (who will be) humble towards the faithful, stern towards the faithless, waging jihad in the way of Allah, not fearing the blame of any blamer (5:54); Allah has promised those of you who have faith and do righteous deeds that He will surely make them successors in the earth, just as He made those who were before them successors, and He will surely establish for them their religion which He has approved for them, and that He will surely change their state to security after their fear, while they worship M e, not ascribing any partners to M e (24:55).

This interpretation is also acceptable.

Another reading of this verse is that umma here refers to a group of people who will be brought forth by God after these disbelievers, but they will persist in their denial of the truth, so God will punish them by eradicating them from the face of the earth, just as it happened to the people of

Noah. Alternatively, umma could refer to the people who come after these disbelievers, and they will persist in disobeying God so that God brings down the Day of Judgement upon them.

However, both of these readings are unfounded, as they both rest on the assumption that the ones being punished are not the disbelievers who are mocking God and the Prophet, while the apparent meaning of God’s words, On the day it overtakes them it shall not be turned away from them, and they will be besieged by what they used to deride, indicates that those who will be punished are the ones who mocked God with their words, ‘W hat holds it back?’

On the day it overtakes them it shall not be turned away from them, and they will be besieged by what they used to deride: This serves the response to their mockery, W hat holds it back?’ And this mockery was their response to the threat of divine punishment. In short, what they are saying is: ‘If the punishment you threaten us with is genuine (and not a fabrication you have contrived), there would be no reason to hold it back, for we

will not give up our disbelief nor turn aside from our religion. Therefore, there is no reason to delay it. On the contrary, you should be hastening to punish us! This shows that your threat is false.’

God responds to this by saying that the punishment will indeed befall them, and on that day, there will be no one who can defiect it. This torment, which they mock, will ultimately encompass them.

Based on what has been previously mentioned, it appears that the punishment they are threatened with is worldly; it will envelop them and descend upon them in addition to the torment of the Hereafter. Therefore, this verse and one before it each describe something that the disbelievers imagine in their ignorance. The previous verse mentions that when they are reminded of the Resurrection and warned about the punishment that awaits them on the Day of Judgement, they say: ‘This is nothing but plain magic.’ The present verse mentions that when God delays their punishment for a time and they are informed of this, they mockingly say: ‘What

holds it back?’

(11:9) If We let man taste (adhaqnā) a mercy from Us, and then withdraw (nazaʿnā-hā) it from him, he becomes despondent (yaʾūs), ungrateful.

In M ajmaʿ al-bayān, al-Ṭabrisī writes:

‘Taste (dhawq) means to put something into one’s mouth to ascertain its fiavour. God refers to the granting of pleasures to human beings “tasting” because of how quickly they vanish like things that are tasted and then disappear. This is similar to the saying, “dreams of sleep are like a fieeting shadow.” To withdraw something (nazaʿ) means to pull something from its place, to be despondent. yaʾs, (from which yaʾūs is derived) means to be certain that something desired will not occur, the opposite of this is hope.’ In this verse, God substitutes mercy (raḥma) for blessings to show that the blessings He gives to humans are a form of mercy, which means to fulfil human needs without their having done anything to deserve this or without any obligation. Therefore, the meaning of the verse is: ‘If we grant man something of the blessings that he enjoys and then We withdraw it, he becomes hopeless and his despair intensifies to the point where he believes it is impossible that it will ever be restored to him, and he becomes ungrateful for our blessings, as if he views those blessings as his inherent right and

does not believe they belong to Us. So, humans are prone to despairing about what is taken from them and being ungrateful.’ Note that the term “man” is used in the verse, indicating the entire human race, to show that these characteristics is a trait of the human species.

(11:10) And if W e let him have a taste of blessings (naʿmāʾ) after adversities have befallen him, he will surely say, ‘All ills have left me.’ Indeed he becomes an exultant braggart, Al-Ṭabrisī says in M ajmaʿ al-bayān:

‘Blessings (naʿmāʾ) are favors whose effects are visible in the one who receives them, while adversities (darrāʾ) are visible sources of harm. This is because these two words are conjugated according to the same pattern as words such as hamrāʾ (‘red’) and ʿaynāʾ (‘verdent’), which concern outward and visible states. ‘Joy’ (faraḥ) and ‘delight’ (surūr) are similar in that they represent an openness of heart to what one enjoys, the opposite of which is sorrow… a braggart (fakhūr) is someone who frequently boasts and extols his own virtues, which is considered a negative trait when mentioned without any context because it implies behaving arrogantly

towards those who do not deserve such treatment.’

In this context, the meaning of ‘ills’ (sayyiʾāt) is the calamities and disasters that afflict man, causing him distress. The meaning then is: ‘If We bless him with prosperity after adversity, he will certainly say, “M y troubles have left me.”’ This implies a belief that those hardships and adversities will not return once they have disappeared, and will not befall him again after they have been lifted.

The phrase, indeed he becomes an exultant braggart, provides a rationale for his saying, ‘All ills have left me.’ This is because he exults and

continues to exult as he tastes blessings after adversity. On the other hand, if he recognized that the blessings he enjoys might vanish and could not be counted on to remain, and that he doesn’t have control over them but someone else does, and that it’s possible for the ills he has experienced to return, he wouldn’t exult in this way. For there is no joy in transient and unsettled matters.

Moreover, he boasts about the blessings he has been given over others. However, a person cannot boast unless it is about an honor or virtue

that they possess. So, it is because he sees his blessings as matters under his control, things that others cannot take from him, and that no one cannot bring back the ills he previously suffered, that he boasts and goes to

extremes in boasting.

(11:11) excepting those who are patient and do righteous deeds. For such there will be forgiveness and a great reward.

God points out the typical human reactions to hardship and disaster, which are despair and ingratitude, and to prosperity and blessings, which are joy and boasting. The implication is that humans have a short-sighted perspective, seeing only what is immediately before them and being bewildered by anything beyond that. If a blessing is taken from a person, he

doesn’t believe it will ever return and forgets that it was from God, who has the power to restore it to him if He wills. If he remembered that all blessings were ultimately from God, this would encourage him to be steadfast

in adversity and to turn his heart to God in hope and supplication. On the other hand, if a blessing is restored to him after he has been deprived of it, he believes that it is his rightful due, so he rejoices and boasts, failing

to see God’s hand in it to give thanks to Him for it, and does not restrain his joy or cease extolling his own superiority over others.

However, God exempts a group of humans from this general pattern, describing them with the phrase, those who are patient and do righteous deeds, and then promises them a great reward with the phrase, For such there will be forgiveness and a great reward. This is because escaping from this blameworthy tendency is only possible for those who are steadfast in times of adversity— so that their distress does not drive them to despair and ingratitude—and who do good deeds—by thanking God for removing adversity and replacing it with blessings— and using His blessings in ways that please Him and benefit His creatures, so that feelings of self-sufficiency do not give way to joy and boasting.

These are the ones who are truly saved, their Lord will forgive them by erasing traces of the reprehensible tendency towards short-sightedness and replacing it with praiseworthy qualities, and they will have great forgiveness and reward from their Lord.

The verse provides evidence that patience combined with good deeds is inseparable from faith, as it promises these patient ones forgiveness and great reward, and forgiveness is not granted to idolaters. God says, Indeed Allah does not forgive that any partner should be ascribed to Him (4:116). The promise of forgiveness and a great reward, exactly as mentioned in this verse, is also given to the believers in the verse, There is a severe punishment for the faithless, but for those who have faith and do righteous deeds there will be forgiveness and a great reward (35:7), and in the verse, Indeed for those who fear their Lord in secret there will be forgiveness and a great reward (67:12).

The connection of these three verses with what precedes them is clear, as the discussion in the previous verses was leading up to the disbelief of the disbelievers, their mockery of the promise of Resurrection, and their responding to the threat of punishment with ridicule. God points out that they, in their natural state, do not believe that the blessings they have from God will ever come to an end due to the descent of punishment, nor will whatever miseries that have befallen them change into a pleasant life and the good enjoyments that God promised them at the beginning of the chapter.

(11:12) Lest you should disregard aught of what has been revealed to you, and be upset by it because they say, ‘W hy has not a treasure been sent down to him, or not an angel accompany him?’ You are only a warner, and Allah is a trustee over all things.

Since the Prophet’s message is supported by the Qurʾan, clear signs, proofs, and decisive evidences, that no sane person could deny it and no human being with sense could reject or disbelieve in it, therefore, the Qurʾan’s account of the disbelief of the disbelievers and denial of the polytheists seems highly unlikely by nature. When an event is highly unlikely

to occur, a person will often seek some explanation of why it has happened in order to avoid simply acknowledging that something improbable has come to pass.

This is the context in which the present verses must be understood. Taking into account what God has related about the disbelievers’ denial and the idolaters rejection of what the Prophet brought to them in terms of the clear truth and divine message that were revealed to him, along with the clear evidences and arguments that could not be denied or rejected, God considers the issue from several perspectives to provoke reflection. For example, He says in the present verse, Lest you should disregard aught of what has been revealed to you … and in the next one, Do they say, ‘He has fabricated it … ?’

It is as if to say: ‘It is highly improbable that you guide them to the manifest truth and they hear My words from you, and then they do not respond to your call and deny the truth after it has become clear to them. Perhaps you have omitted some of what is revealed to you and failed to invite them to it, and that is why they have confronted you with denial? Or do they claim that the Qurʾan is not the word of God, but rather it is a fabrication you have concocted in His name, and that is why they did not believe in it? If you have left out some of the revelation for fear that they might challenge you with the verses, remember, you are just a warner, and you have no control over what God wills. If they claim that it is a fabrication, then ask them to produce ten chapters like it, fabricated.’

From what has been previously discussed, it is evident that the tone of this verse is hypothetical, in light of the highly improbable nature of this outcome. In this case, every potential reason that might bring about the unlikely event is considered. This is analogous to the case of a king, some of whose weak subjects have rebelled against him. He sends one of his agents to call them to hear and obey and writes a letter that he commands his messenger to read to the rebels. The letter criticizes his subjects

for their rebellion and arrogance, for daring to take up arms despite their weakness and abasement and his strength, authority, and honor. Then the king receives a report that they rejected his messenger and the message he brought. So, the king writes a second letter, and commands that it be read to them. The second letter says to the messenger, ‘perhaps you did not read my letter to them for fear that they might challenge you with something you cannot handle, or that they claim that the letter is not from me, but you have fabricated it. If the first is the case, you are just a messenger, and your only duty is to convey the message. If the second, then the letter is in my handwriting, written by my hand, sealed with my seal, and no one other than me can replicate that.’

Reflecting on this example shows that the tone conveyed by the second letter is one of improbability, and the purpose of mentioning the two

possibilities— failing to deliver the full message and the claim of fabrication—is not to reprimand the messenger or give any serious consideration

their claims of falsehood and trickery. Instead, these two possibilities are mentioned as a preliminary step to clarifying these doubts, namely that the messenger has no control over the matter in order to manipulate it, and there is no doubt or uncertainty in the message of the king.

Based on this reflection, it is obvious that when God says: Lest you should disregard aught of what has been revealed to you, and be upset because they say…, this doesn’t seriously suggest that the Prophet has failed to convey God’s message or that he should be reprimanded in any way. Nor is

it intended to console him or soothe the feelings of sorrow or distress he experiences because of their disbelief and denial of the clear truth he has brought them. Instead, the speech is leading towards the words: You are only a warner, and Allah is a trustee over all things.

Some commentators have argued that the speech is intended to forbid the Prophet from feeling sorrow or distress due to the disbelief and denial of the idolaters, and that this prohibition is supposed to console him and give him peace of mind, similar to the verse: And do not grieve for them, nor be upset by their guile (16:127), and the verse,: You are liable to imperil your life (out of distress) that they will not have faith. If We wish We will send down to them a sign from the sky before which their heads will remain bowed in humility (26:3–4). However, this interpretation does not fit with the context of the verse.

It is also evident that His saying, Lest you should disregard …, and His saying, “Do they say, ‘He has fabricated it …?’ are two parts of a refutation and they are both connected together with what preceded them in the same way, as we have already mentioned.

The passage, Lest you should disregard aught of what has been revealed to you … says ‘aught’ (in other words, ‘some’) because the preceding verses confirm that the Prophet has conveyed the message in general. So perhaps, this verse suggests to the Prophet, you have left out some of what We have revealed to you in the Qurʾan, so you haven’t recited it to them, so the truth is not completely unveiled to them, because you did not want them confront you with the denial and rejection that they have confronted you with anyway. This is because one part of the Qurʾan clarifies another part, and one passage of it renders another more acceptable— the verses containing arguments clarify the verses containing claims, and verses of reward

and punishment make people more likely to accept the truth through encouragement and warnings, while verses of stories and parables appeal to people’s psyches and soften their hearts.

As for the phrase, ‘and be upset by it because they say …’(ḍāʾiq bihi ṣadruka an yaqūlū …, lit. ‘and your chest should tighten because they say…’), al-Ṭabrisī says in M ajmaʿ al-bayān:

‘The word ḍāʾiq (‘tightened’— an active participle of the verb ḍāqa) here means the same as ‘tight’ (ḍayq—the infinitive of the same verb), but ḍāʾiq is used here for two reasons: first, because it is more fitting in the context, and second, because of the assonance between it and the Arabic word ‘disregard’ (tārik—as both words share the same pattern of conjugation).’

It appears that the pronoun ‘it’ in ‘by it’ (bihi) refers back to aught of what has been revealed to you. Although some commentators have suggested that the pronoun actually refers to their statement, W hy has not

a treasure been sent down to him…? or to the fact that they are making such demands. This aligns better with the phrase, because they say, acting as a substitution (badal) for the pronoun in ‘it.’ However, our explanation aligns better with it acting as the object of the verb ‘disregard.’ The

implied meaning is: ‘perhaps you would disregard this out of fear that they will say, “Why hasn’t a treasure been sent down to him or an angel come with him?”’

The phrase, You are only a warner is a response to the impertinent demands of the idolaters, Why has not a treasure been sent down to him, or not an angel accompany him? God has repeatedly mentioned these demands of theirs in various contexts, sometimes focusing solely on the appearance of an angel and others adding more elements to it. For example, they sometimes demand that God Himself should appear to bear witness to the truthfulness of his message, or that the Prophet should have a heavenly garden from which to eat, or that a book should descend from the

heavens that they all can read. God has responded to all of these demands in a similar way as here, stating that His messenger has only the message to deliver. Being a human messenger, it is not within his power to accede to their suggestions unless God wills it and authorizes a sign, as He has said elsewhere, A messenger may not bring any sign except by Allah’s permission (40:78).

Then, after saying, You are only a warner, God adds, and Allah is a trustee over all things. This completes His response to their demands that the Prophet produce miracles in response to their whims. In other words, the Prophet is a human being like them, and he has not been commanded to do anything other than to deliver a warning, which is a message informing someone of danger. The direction and governance of all affairs, whether

following their natural course or breaking the natural order of things, falls to God alone, so there is no basis for them to assign responsibility for these things to the Prophet when they are matters beyond his control.

This is because God is the creator of all things and their originator, and He is the one who manages everything according to its established order. There is nothing except that He is the initiator of its affair and its final destination, whether things are occurring naturally or breaking the natural order. He is the one who is entrusted with its matter and manages its affair, and so He is the trustee over all things. A trustee (wakīl) is someone who is entrusted with a matter and looks after it. Therefore, God Almighty is the trustee over all things.

Based on this, it is apparent that the statement, and Allah is a trustee over all things, when combined with, You are only a warner, serves to constrain the focus of the passage, as they asked the Prophet for something

that does not belong to him, but rather belongs to God Almighty.

(11:13) Or do they say, ‘He has fabricated it’? Say, ‘Then bring ten chapters like it, fabricated, and invoke whomever you can, besides Allah, should you be truthful.’

We have already discussed the possibility of reading ‘or’ (am) being connected to the statement, Lest you should disregard…, in the sense of a question. The implication being, ‘Are you omitting some of what has been revealed to you out of fear that they will demand a miracle? Or do they say that you have fabricated it and falsely ascribed it to us? For it is unlikely that they would hear my words, then not believe in them.’ Some commentators have said that ‘or’ is detached and not intended a question. This would render the meaning: ‘Rather, they say he invented it.’

The Qur’anic Challenge:1

Say, ‘Then bring ten chapters like it, fabricated …’: This is a clear challenge. The pronoun ‘it’ in ‘like it’ (mithli-hi) refers back to the Qurʾan or the chapter insofar as it is part of the Qurʾan. The preposition ‘then’ (fa) in ‘then bring’ (fa-ʾtū) shows that this challenge is in response to their claim, ‘He has fabricated it.’ Note that this statement is abridged for the sake of brevity, its full implication being: ‘If this Qurʾan is what I fabricated and falsely ascribed to God, then it is something I have produced from myself. Therefore, it should be possible for someone else to come up with something like it. If you are truthful in your claims and serious, not jesting, then bring ten chapters like it, invented, and seek help in that with the

invocation of all those you can besides God from your idols, which you claim to be gods and to which you rush for all your needs, and others from the rest of the humankind until you have tried all means and methods at your disposal, and there remains no one from whom you can expect aid or assistance in accomplishing this. If this was truly from me, not from God, it would be possible for you to bring something like it then.’

This explanation reveals that the challenge presented by the Qurʾan in this verse does not only refer to its arrangement and eloquence, as God

1 We have added this heading because of the nature of the discussion regarding the challenge offered by the Qur’an under the verse 11:13. (Pub.)

tells them to seek assistance from anyone who they could call upon besides God, whether their idols or other creatures, including those who do not know the Arabic language, who are not fiuent in its composition, or aware of its eloquence. Therefore, the challenge is general, encompassing all of the Qurʾan’s contents, including authentic teachings, clear arguments, manifest proofs, virtuous admonitions, noble morals, knowledge of the unseen, as well as fiuency and eloquence in Arabic. This is akin to the verse, Say, ‘Should all humans and jinn rally to bring the like of this Qurʾan, they will not bring the like of it, even if they assisted one another’ (17:88). We have already addressed this topic in our discussion on the miraculous inimitability of the Qurʾan.

From this, it is clear that the miraculous nature of the Qurʾan does not lie solely in its eloquence, clarity, or unique arrangement. Were this not the case, the challenge would not be limited to mere falsification and fabrication, because rhetoric (balāgha) has three levels. The highest of these tiers

is miraculous and beyond human capabilities, while the middle and lower tiers are within the capacity of ordinary human beings. Therefore, the challenge in the verse only applies to the highest of these levels. However, if the miraculous nature of the Qurʾan referred only to eloquence, then even the most inarticulate speech could have been potentially more eloquent and miraculous.

The alikeness mentioned in the verse (‘like it’) also cannot refer to mere genre similarity, as such similarity would imply imitation, which would not constitute an answer to the challenge. Rather, in this, it goes back to the conventions of Arabic literature, as we can see in the poetic duels of Imruʾ al-Qays and ʿAlqama, ʿUmar b. Kulthūm and al-Ḥārith b. Halza, and Jarīr and al-Farazdaq.

This discussion illustrates, firstly, that if the miraculous aspect of the Qurʾan were its linguistic eloquence alone, something only Arabs would understand, then involving non-Arabs in the challenge would be meaningless. Equally, the verses, … and invoke whomever you can, besides Allah, with

its generality, and similarly the verse, Should all humans and jinn rally …, would not have had any meaningful purpose. On the contrary, it would have made more sense to say, ‘If all Arabs rally …’ or ‘Call upon whom you can from your idols and your fellow speakers …’

Secondly, it shows that if the miraculous aspect of the Qurʾan was solely located in its eloquence, then the argument found in verses such as Had it been from other than Allah, they would have surely found much discrepancy in it (4:82) would be not have made any sense. This verse appears to deny all forms of contradiction, but most contradictions, which relate to ideas, do not harm the linguistic eloquence of expression. This is supported by the verse in this chapter: Then bring ten chapters like it, fabricated, and invoke whomever you can, besides Allah … If the Qurʾan’s miraculous aspect were exclusively to be found in its eloquence, these challenges would be beyond the natural sequence.

Thirdly, God issues a challenge with His statement: Let them bring a discourse like it (52:34), and His statement in Sūrah Yūnus: Then bring a chapter like it, and invoke whomever you can, besides Allah (10:38). We have already inferred in our previous discussions that Sūrah Yūnus was revealed before Sūrah Hūd, as supported by traditions. Then, in this chapter, God says: Then bring ten chapters like it, fabricated, and invoke whomever you can, besides Allah. If the miraculous nature of the Qurʾan were exclusively due to its eloquence, these challenges would not have followed their

appropriate natural sequence, as it would not be right to burden men of eloquence among the Arabs, who deny that the Qurʾan is from God, with producing a chapter like it, and then producing ten fabricated chapters like it. It would be more natural to challenge them to produce the entirety of the Qurʾan. If they fail in that, then to produce ten chapters like it, fabricated. Then, if they fail again, then to produce a chapter like it.

Some scholars have addressed this issue by explaining that the order of the chapters and the revelation of some of these before others does not necessarily determine the sequence of the verses within these chapters. After all, there are many M eccan verses located within M edinan chapters and vice versa. Therefore, it is conceivable that the challenge verses pertaining to the entirety of the Qurʾan were revealed before others. Then,

the verse challenging to produce ten fabricated chapters could have been revealed after that, and the verse challenging to produce a single chapter could have been revealed last of all.

This approach would be plausible if we accept that the verses were revealed as described. Otherwise, the issue remains unresolved. The truth is that the Qurʾan is miraculous in all of its unique attributes, including its eloquence, clarity, authentic teachings, noble ethics, divine laws, narratives, parables, knowledge of the unseen, as well as its power over hearts and its beauty that overawes peoples’ souls.

As for the challenge to produce ten chapters, given the challenge presented in Sūrah Yūnus to produce just one, al-Ṭabrisī writes in Majmaʿ

al-Bayān:

‘If one were to ask, “Why is the challenge of the Qurʾan sometimes to produce ten chapters, sometimes one chapter, and sometimes with a discourse like it?” The answer is that the challenge pertains to the manifestations of the Qurʾan’s miraculous nature seen in the arrangement of its speech. Therefore, it is possible to challenge the audience with more or less.’

To this, I would add that, while this explanation is suitable for the principle of challenging its opponents with either one or many, the challenge of producing ten chapters after the challenge of producing one,

especially considering the view that its miraculous nature is based solely on eloquence, is not convincing.

Other scholars have sought to explain this by saying that the Qurʾan is miraculous in all that it contains, including knowledge, ethics, rulings, stories, and more, characterized by eloquence, rhetoric, and the absence of any discrepancy. The real test occurs when an opponent can bring several chapters similar to the Qurʾan, and in those chapters, no difference is seen, especially if those chapters contain stories, demonstrate both eloquence and rhetorical brilliance, and communicate teachings. Only under these circumstances could it be proven that the Qurʾan is not a miracle. However, this cannot be established by presenting only one chapter.

This can only be accomplished by presenting equivalents of the longer chapters that encompass all of the aforementioned features, including

knowledge, narratives, arguments, and more, like the chapters al-Aʿrāf and al-Anʿām.

The long chapters of the Qurʾan that were revealed, encompassing all the aforementioned features before Sūrah Hūd, according to the traditions, are Sūrah al-Aʿrāf, Sūrah Yūnus, Sūrah Maryam, Sūrah Ṭa Ha,

Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ, Sūrah al-Naml, Sūrah al-Qaṣaṣ, Sūrah al-Qamar, and

Sūrah Ṣād. These nine chapters, together with Sūrah Hūd, make up ten, which aligns with the challenge to produce ten fabricated chapters like them. This is a summarized explanation— the author’s original discussion was more expansive.

Author’s comment:

First, one should not rely heavily on traditions to determine the order of the revelation of the Qurʾan’s chapters. These are, after all, solitary reports that are often of uncertain reliability, and it is not advisable to base exegetical research on such reports.

Second, the apparent meaning of the statement, Or do they say, ‘He has fabricated it’? Say, ‘Then bring ten chapters like it, fabricated …’ (11:13), indicates that their accusation of the Prophet fabricating lies about God concerns all the chapters of the Qurʾan, both long and short, without specifying one or the other. Therefore, they are obligated to provide a decisive response regarding every Qurʾanic chapter, and the challenge is what fulfils this. If they were unable to produce ten long fabricated chapters that encompass the features of the Qurʾan, it does not confirm that

all of its chapters, even short ones like al-Kawthar and al-ʿAsr, are from God, unless some additional argument is made, but the text is devoid of any such argument.

Thirdly, regarding the phrase ten chapters like it, if the pronoun ‘it’ refers to the Qurʾan, as appears to be the case in the speaker’s statement, this suggests that the challenge to produce ten fabricated chapters like it is without restriction, whether they are long or short. To restrict the challenge to ten long chapters would be to arbitrarily restrict the meaning of

the verse without textual evidence, and it would be even more restrictive to claim that the intended comparison is with the ten chapters listed above. If, on the other hand, the pronoun refers to Sūrah Hūd, this would seem like an odd stipulation. How can it be said to someone who claims that Sūrah al-Kawthar, Sūrah al-Falaq, and Sūrah al-Nās are fabrications against God to produce ten fabricated chapters like Sūrah Hūd and restrict it to that? Unless they argue that this chapter alone is a fabrication against God, in which case the challenge would then be to produce its like. Yet, we have never come across anyone who made such a claim.

Let us now turn to the visible differences between the challenge verses such as, then bring a chapter like it (10:38); where the challenge seems to be for them to produce a single chapter, or then bring ten chapters like it, fabricated (11:13); where the challenge seems to be for a specific number above one, or bring a discourse like it (52:34), where the challenge seems to be for a dialogue that is similar to the Qurʾan, even if it is less than a whole chapter. Each of these verses serves a specific purpose in the Qurʾan’s challenge to humankind.

To explain further: The various aspects and features of the Qurʾan, which constitute its truth as a divine book, in addition to its eloquent language and rhetorical composition, are related to its meanings and intentions. By ‘meaning’ (maʿnā), I do not mean what rhetoricians intend when

they say that eloquence is an attribute of meaning (al-balāgha min ṣifāt al-maʿnā) and words are merely a medium. By this, they mean the ideas as they are naturally organized in the mind. However, what they refer to as ‘meaning’ can be found in plain lies, jests, obscenities, satire, and fabrications if they are expressed eloquently, and can be found abundantly in

inherited compositions of eloquent poets and prose writers.

Rather, the meaning and purpose of the Qurʾan are what God describes it as: A wise book, a clear light, a great Qurʾan, a criterion, a guide leading to truth, a straight path, a decisive word, and not a jest; a mighty book that falsehood cannot approach from before it or from behind, a remembrance that judges among people in what they differ about. It is a healing and mercy for the believers and it does not increase the wrongdoers except in loss. It is a clarification for everything and none can touch it except the purified.

It is clear that all these are attributes of the meaning of the Qurʾan, rather than its text. They are not characteristics of what rhetoricians mean by the ‘eloquence’, which can also be found in falsehoods in speech that the noble Qurʾan refers to as frivolous discourse and sin; it warns against engaging in or uttering them, even if they are examples of eloquent speech. The meaning endowed with these attributes is part of the divine intentions that proceed on the basis of truth, untainted by falsehood, falling within the path of guidance. The discourse that encompasses this meaning, the attribute, and the purpose of this matter, is the one to which divine care is attached, making it a mercy for the believers and a reminder to the worlds. It is this aspect of the Qurʾan with which it is suitable to challenge the disbelievers in the likes of the phrase, let them bring a discourse like (52:34). We do not call an utterance a ‘discourse’ (ḥadīth) unless it encompasses a significant purpose which it expresses and conveys from one mind to another. Similarly, in the phrase, then bring a chapter like it (10:38), God does not mention a collection of verses from the Qurʾan, however numerous, a ‘chapter’ (sūrah) unless they are united by a divine purpose that

distinguishes them from other such collections of verses.

Were this not the case, the challenge could not be accomplished with Qurʾanic verses, and the opponent would be able to choose from a large number of individual verses, such as By the morning brightness, By time, By the mount, In a well-guarded book, Dark green, The Inevitable, W hat is the Inevitable, and what will make you realize what the Inevitable is?, The Most Merciful, The Sovereign of mankind, The God of mankind, And the moon darkens, Nay, and by the moon, We shall summon the guards of Hell, and other individual verses. Then match each of them with corresponding Arabic speech without ensuring a connection between them or including a purpose that unifies and presents them in the form of a single text. What the opponent is tasked with in these challenges is to produce a discourse resembling the Qurʾan, in addition to its eloquent expression, illustrating some of the divine objectives that include purposes characterized by the attributes that God Almighty has mentioned.

The divine discourse, along with the challenge it presents in these verses, differs according to what is manifest of its unique qualities. The entirety of the noble Qurʾan is distinguished by being a book containing everything that humanity requires until the Day of Resurrection, including fundamental knowledge, noble ethics, and subsidiary laws. A chapter

of the Qurʾan is distinguished by the fact that it delivers a comprehensive exposition of a particular purpose among the divine objectives related to the guidance of humankind and the true religion through its exceptional eloquence. This is a level of specificity that is different from that of the entirety of the Qurʾan. A set of chapters, like ten or twenty of them, are characterized by another distinctiveness, demonstrating the diversity of intentions, purposes, and the variety therein. Therefore, it is unlikely that such a stunning work of literature came about by chance.

However, if an opponent is incapable of producing a single chapter, it is conceivable that he may think his inability to do so merely indicates humankind’s inability to do the same, not that the Qurʾan was necessarily revealed by God or revealed through His knowledge. It is possible that

this could be like other cases of human genius or excellence, where one individual might excel in a certain aspect, such as being the tallest, largest, bravest, most generous, most cowardly, or most miserly. Therefore, according to this opponent, the Qurʾan is still the product of a human being,

albeit one who is unmatched in genius.

Now, this possibility is refuted for even a single chapter of the Qurʾan, which is what the opponent intended to challenge (for it is a profoundly eloquent discourse, containing truthful meanings and endowed with noble attributes that is utterly free from the substance of lies). Such a feature does not occur by mere coincidence or happenstance without it being intended in itself, serving a purpose related to the Divine W ill. However, the likelihood of coincidence or happenstance is even more remote when there are

multiple chapters with these features. The production one chapter after another, the exposition of one purpose after another, and the revelation of one secret after another, leaves no room for the possibility of coincidence or happenstance, as should be obvious.

Having clarified the above, it becomes evident that this challenge could also be presented in the form of the verse, Say, ‘Should all humans and jinn rally to bring the like of this Qurʾan, they will not bring the like of it, even if

they assisted one another’ (17:88). In fact, the verse just quoted serves as an introduction to the challenge with the entirety of the Qurʾan due to the divine objectives it encompasses and because it is unique in that it contains everything that humankind will need until the Day of Resurrection. The verse, Say, ‘Then bring a chapter like it …’ (10:38), explicitly challenges the audience to produce a single chapter because each individual chapter of the Qurʾan thoroughly expounds a specific divine purpose that fits into God’s plan for the guidance of humankind without frivolity. Then, the present verse, Say, ‘Then bring ten chapters like it, fabricated…’ challenges them with the production of ten chapters of the Qurʾan, because these both embody a mastery of exposition and a diversity of purpose. Indeed, the number ‘ten’ serves to signify abundance rather than the literal number ten (like ‘a hundred’ or ‘a thousand’), as per the verse: Each of them

is eager to live a thousand years … (2:96). Therefore, what is meant by ten chapters here is ‘a number of chapters’, signifying any quantity that would be recognized as a multitude by the people. It is, as if to say, ‘bring forth a multitude of chapters equivalent to these, a dozen of them.’ This is to make clear that the variety of objectives found in the Qurʾan’s exposition and miraculous discourse can have only come from God.

As for the verse, Let them bring a discourse like it (52:34), this appears to be a challenge that encompasses all of the three aforementioned challenges, as the term discourse can refer to the entirety of the Qurʾan, a single

chapter of it, or ten chapters of it equally. Therefore, this is a challenge to produce anything at all that exhibits the same unique qualities as the Qurʾan, as is obvious.

There remain two matters to address. First, none of the verses challenging adversaries to produce something similar to the Qurʾan describe

the work of adversaries as ‘fabrications’, except for the present one, where it says: Then bring ten chapters like it, fabricated, unlike when it says, Then bring a chapter like it …,where it doesn’t add the adjective ‘fabricated’, as is the case with the remainder of the challenge verses.

The reason behind this, possibly, is that the nature of the concern in the verse under discussion is different from that of the rest of the challenge verses. The emphasis in the rest of the verses is that they are incapable of producing anything like the Qurʾan or even a chapter like it, because the Qurʾan possesses qualities that are beyond human capabilities to imitate and are only found in something of divine origin. By contrast, the present challenge concludes with the phrase, know that it has been sent down

with Allah’s knowledge. This suggests that the challenge here is to create a Qurʾan which contains special divine knowledge, which is beyond the reach of any ordinary person. This is a task that inherently rejects fabrication. It is as though the verse is saying: ‘This Qurʾan cannot be fabricated

as it contains aspects of divine knowledge inaccessible to anyone but God. If you have doubts about this, produce ten fabricated chapters similar to it and seek assistance from anyone you can besides God. If you are unable to do so, know that the unique knowledge found here is exclusive to God.’ So ponder on this.

The second matter is the meaning of the challenge ‘to produce the like of’ something (rather than, say, something ‘better’ than it), where it says the like of this Qurʾan, a discourse like it, a chapter like it, or ten chapters like it.

The apparent reason for this is that, because the discourse is a miraculous sign, if a human could produce something equivalent to it, that would suffice to disprove its miraculous nature, without the need to produce something that excels it in qualities or surpasses it in its unique features. Now, one might argue that the inability of others apart from the Prophet to replicate the Qurʾan does not necessarily demonstrate its miraculous nature or conclusively establish its divine origin. Indeed, attributes

of excellence present in humans, such as eloquence, writing, bravery, generosity, and so on, exist at different varying levels, some surpassing others.

If so, among these levels, there is one that surpasses all others, and it is the utmost level the human mind can aspire to.

For every excellence, there always exists among those possessing it an individual who holds the highest degree of it, unmatched and unchallenged by anyone else. Therefore, among all humans, there will necessarily be someone who is the most eloquent, the most literate, the bravest,

the most generous, the tallest, or the largest, for instance. W hy then can the Prophet not simply have been the most articulate and eloquent of all people, and his Qurʾanic revelation, which no one can counter due to its unmatched nature, be merely his own words? If so, the inability of others to replicate it does not necessarily prove that it is a divine text, as it could still be a unique human text that only he had the ability to produce and elusive to others.

This argument can be countered by stating that human attributes in which differences occur, while existing as mentioned, are natural qualities. These are granted by God’s instillation of potentiality within human

nature, emerging spontaneously and not predicated on coincidence or cause. An individual possessing a characteristic can attribute it to themselves without cause. Given this, if a human individual excels in a particular

virtue and is unmatched and unsurpassed by any other, others still have the option to follow their path and, through practice, training, and discipline, perform acts that mirror the excellence this person appears to exclusively possess, emulating some of their deeds even if they cannot compete with them entirely or equal them in every aspect. Thus, the distinguished individual will retain a unique position of originality and precedence, but

others will still clearly be able to come close to them.

Take, for instance, the pre-Islamic figure of Ḥātim, who was known for his generosity. Even though he was unrivalled and unmatched in his generosity, it was still possible for others to follow in his footsteps, practicing and training themselves to manifest some level of his generosity, even if

they could not rival him entirely or practice it at his legendary level. This is the case for all human virtues and the principle that governs all human actions. Through practice and training, humans can follow the path of pioneers in these virtues and perform some of their deeds, even if they cannot match their original standing entirely.

However, if we were to assume that the Qurʾan is the Prophet’s speech, rather than that of God, and that he is potentially the most eloquent and rhetorically gifted human to have ever lived, it would be plausible that others could take interest, train, and attempt to imitate the sublime patterns

he originated in his speech. They might be able to imitate something of the text, to produce a chapter like it, even if they couldn’t replicate the entirety of the Qurʾan. After all, the challenge issued in the aforementioned verses does not require that they to come up with a more eloquent or superior discourse, or a more eloquent or superior chapter, to the point where the Qurʾan is regarded as the most eloquent or the best human speech and there is nothing more eloquent or superior to it. In which case, their inability to produce such doesn’t indicate that it is not of human origin. Rather, what was actually said was: Let them bring a discourse like it, Say, ‘Then bring a chapter like it …’, and so forth. Humans are, after all, capable of replicating human speech, even if we suppose that no one else can rival it. As we

have already explained, the doubt is dispelled by God’s use of the phrase ‘like it’ (mithli-hi), as if the Qurʾan was human speech, they should have been able to at least imitate it.

Commentary continues:

(11:14) But if they do not respond to you, know that it has been sent down with Allah’s knowledge, and that there is no god except Him. W ill you, then, submit?

From the context, it appears that the verse is addressing the idolaters, and that it is part of the Prophet’s speech included within the command ‘Say …’ in the previous verse, which God bid him to convey to them. Therefore, the plural pronoun ‘they’ in If they do not respond … refers back to the idols and everyone they sought help from besides God, indicated by His words: and invoke whomever you can, besides Allah.

The implication is: ‘If those helpers whom you called upon—your deities, your men of eloquence who are well-versed in the artful use of language, the scholars of the People of the Book who are in possession of divine scriptures containing the tales of prophets and nations, soothsayers who are inspired by the whisperings of demons, learned persons, and

other people immersed in human knowledge—do not respond to your call, O idolaters, then know that this Qurʾan has been revealed with God’s knowledge. It was not something I produced from my knowledge or the knowledge of anyone else whom you allege to have taught it me!

And know that what I invite you to—monotheism—is the truth. For if there were any deity other than God, they would have supported you in what you invited them to. So, are you polytheists willing to submit to God, obedient to His command?’

Therefore, God’s statement, But if they do not respond to you …, means as we might say, ‘if you still cannot meet this challenge after seeking help and support from whomever you could invoke other than God …’ This is because the reasons that necessitate their capability to meet this challenge are their eloquent language and rhetorical skill. They believe that these qualities are gifts from their deities besides God, and also gifts that their deities have not yet bestowed upon them. Now, according to this belief of theirs, these deities could have supported them with such gifts if they so chose. Also, they could draw assistance from others besides these deities of theirs. However, if those they call upon do not come to their aid in

meeting the Qurʾan’s challenge, then this shows that the means they have at their disposal are exhausted and, consequently, their capability to meet its challenge is shown to be null. Therefore, the lack of response from their associates in opposing the Qurʾan demonstrates their own incapacity to do so, even when aided by their own intrinsic abilities. This is what the current passage hints at.

When God says, know that it has been sent down with Allah’s knowledge, this refers to God’s unique knowledge, the Unseen (al-ghayb), which

is inaccessible to anyone other than Him, except with His permission. As He has stated elsewhere in the Qurʾan, But Allah bears witness to what He has sent down to you—He sent it down with His knowledge (4:166); These are accounts of the Unseen which We reveal to you (12:102); Knower of the Unseen, He does not disclose His Unseen to anyone, except to a messenger He approves of (72:26–27); and This is indeed a noble Qurʾan, in a guarded Book, no one touches it except the pure ones, gradually sent down from the Lord of all the worlds (56:77–80).

Thus, the meaning is: ‘If you are unable to oppose it through any of the means from which you have sought help besides God, be certain that it was revealed only due to an unseen cause and that it contains knowledge of the Unseen that is known only to God. He is the one who revealed it to me, spoke to me with it, and intended to make me and you understand the true knowledge and treasures of guidance that it contains.’

Some have said that what is intended here is that the Qurʾan was only revealed with God’s knowledge of its revelation and this is His attestation to it being a genuine revelation from Him. Others have suggested that it means the Qurʾan was only revealed with God’s knowledge that it cannot be opposed or with His knowledge of its structure and order, which no one else knows. However, these interpretations are weak and far from a proper understanding of the text.

The phrase, know that it has been sent down with Allah’s knowledge is but the first of two conclusions that are drawn from the failure of the idolater’s confederates to respond to them. The second conclusion is found within the statement, and that there is no god except Him. Both of these conclusions are necessarily arrived at in two ways:

The first is that when the idolaters call upon their deities for matters of concern to them, and these deities do not respond, it reveals that these deities are not truly gods. The true Deity is the one who responds to the distressed when He is called upon, especially when the request is to the benefit of the deity being invoked. The Qurʾan brought by the Prophet was destined to defeat these deities, erase all memory of them from humankind, and turn people away from them. So, if the idolater’s patrons do not

respond when they are called upon to oppose such a book, it is the clearest evidence for the negation of their divinity.

The second way is that if it is established that the Qurʾan is the truth that has been revealed by God and it is veracious in its accounts and it asserts that there is no other deity other than God, then we have no choice but to affirm that there is no god but Him.

His question, W ill you, then, submit?, implies that given all that you have come to know, that your patrons other than God have not responded to you, and that you are fundamentally unable to respond to the Qurʾan’s challenge, will you then submit to this knowledge, which affirms the oneness of God and the fact that the Qurʾan has been revealed with His knowledge? In reality, this command to submit is framed as a question, which is

suggested by the apparent meaning of the verse.

It has also been suggested that the verse, But if they do not respond to you …, is actually God speaking to the Prophet in the plural form to honor him (that is, ‘you’ plural) and elevate his status. Then, the third person plural pronoun (‘they’) refers back to the idolaters, meaning: ‘If the idolaters do not respond to the challenge you, O Prophet, have delivered to them, then know that the Qurʾan is revealed with the knowledge of God, and that God is One. So, will you submit to His command?’

However, the problem with this reading is that, in classical Arabic, only the first-person plural (‘we’) conveys a higher status, and this is specifically for the speaker. The same is not true for the second or third person plurals, ‘you’ (pl.) and ‘they.’

This is in addition to the fact that when God speaks to the Prophet or sends him revelations, there is no question that this comes from Him, such that he would require some evidence for it. The Prophet receives this in a way that he inherently knows it is a speech from God; inherent in the sense that it requires no further proof of its divine origin. Therefore, it is not necessary for God to call the Prophet’s attention to the failure of the idolaters to meet the challenge of the Qurʾan or their inability to do so in order to prove to him that it is indeed His speech. This is unlike the speech of other creatures such as humans, jinn, angels, or any other speaker, which would require some external evidence, through either sensory perception or reason, to confirm that it did indeed come from the speaker. This concept was hinted at in the story of Zechariah in Sūrah Āl ʿImrān, and we

will discuss this more fully later on.

Not to mention that addressing the Prophet with words such as and that there is no god except Him. W ill you, then, submit? does not make sense, and the reasoning behind such a reading is also incomplete, as we will show. Other commentators have suggested that the verse is addressed to both the Prophet and to the totality of the believers or solely to believers because they share with him the role of calling others to the religion and challenging them with the Qurʾan, which is the scripture of their Lord revealed

to them through the Prophet. According to this reading, the meaning of the verse is thus: ‘if the idolaters do not respond to your challenge, then know that the Qurʾan is revealed with the knowledge of God, and there is no god but Him. So, will you all then submit to God?’

However, when some other commentators saw that there is no point in inviting believers— who are already firm in their belief in God alone and His book—to acknowledge that it is a book revealed by God, and that He is One without partner, they proposed a revision to this reading, namely: ‘Be steadfast in your knowledge that it is indeed revealed with the knowledge of God, thereby strengthening your faith and certainty that there is

no deity deserving of worship but Him. Will you then remain steadfast in your submission and dedication to Him?’

However, this reading arbitrarily restricts the scope of the verse’s meaning while presenting an incomplete argument.
