If the idolaters had responded to the Qurʾan’s challenge with all the resources at their disposal, invoking their deities and all those they hoped could help them among jinn and humans, and then failed to meet this challenge, this would have been a clear indication that the Qurʾan was indeed beyond human speech, thereby completing the argument against them. However, the non-response of the unbelievers to the challenge does not prove that it is from God, because they did not attempt what they were challenged to do, namely, then bring ten chapters like it, fabricated.This is either because they knew it was the truth from God (and their accusation of it being forged stemmed from stubbornness and obstinacy, not conviction in this claim or doubt about the Qurʾan) or because they despaired of their partners ever responding to the challenge, or because they were frivolous in their speech, speaking nonsense rather than engaging seriously with the Prophet’s arguments. In sum, the lack of any response from the idolaters to the Prophet or to the believers, or to both, does not, by itself, indicate that the Qurʾan was revealed by God, unless their lack of response occurred after they had called on their associates and patrons to assist them and these associates and patrons did not respond. However, there is no evidence in the verse that the idolaters ever made such a call, so their lack of response alone is not sufficient to show this. The only remaining interpretation would be that the verse means: ‘If the idolaters called upon all those whom they could besides God, and they did not respond, and if the idolaters did not respond to you, O Prophet and believers, then know that the Qurʾan is only revealed with the knowledge of God …’, and this confirms our aforementioned criticism that such a reading arbitrarily restricts the meaning of the verse. This is in addition to the fact that such a reading would mean that the verse implicitly demanded that the believers fortify their faith and certainty based on the non-occurrence of an event— an illogical demand that

is beneath the dignity of God’s speech. Had the verse meant to imply that the idolaters are incapable of meeting the Qurʾan’s challenge even if they call upon all of their associates, it would have been more appropriate to say, ‘But if they do not respond to you, and they will not respond,know …’, similar to the verse where God says, And if you are in doubt concerning what We have sent down to Our servant, then bring a sūrah like it, and invoke your helpers besides Allah, should you be truthful. And if you do not—and you will not—then beware the Fire whose fuel will be humans and stones, prepared for the faithless. (2:23-24).

(11:15-16) As for those who desire the life of this world and its glitter, W e will recompense them fully for their works therein, and

they shall not be underpaid in it. They are the ones for whom there shall be nothing in the Hereafter but Fire: what they had accomplished in the world has failed, and their works have come to naught.

‘Recompense’ (tawfiya) means to deliver a person what they are due in full, without stinting anything from it, while ‘underpaid’ (bakhsh) means to pay someone less than the full amount due to them.

The verse contains a threat for those who do not surrender to the truth when it comes to them and refuse to submit to it, preferring the life of this world and forgetting about the Hereafter. It also elucidates some of the laws of causality that make them despair of the blessings of the Hereafter. This is because any action, no matter what it is, only permits a person to attain the goal for which it was intended. If the goal is worldly, and the action serves the affairs of this life in terms of wealth, beauty, or comfort, then this action— if all other contributing factors are favorable— leads to the outcome that was desired. As for the objectives of the Hereafter, there is nothing to say about them because they were not an outcome intended by the doer of the action, so they do not occur. The mere fact that an action is appropriate for the path of the Hereafter and beneficial for achieving its rewards, such as righteousness, good conduct, and good character, does not necessitate reward and elevation in ranks unless it was intended for the sake of pleasing God and obtaining His reward.

This is why God follows up by saying: They are the ones for whom there shall be nothing in the Hereafter but Fire: what they had accomplished in the world has failed, and their works have come to naught (11:16). This reveals that when they are faced with the life of the Hereafter, they will enter the abode of the reality of their deeds, which is a fire that consumes all of their worldly deeds just as fire consumes firewood, obliterates, and destroys everything that gratifies their souls in the pleasures of existence. It nullifies the effects in the hereafter of all that they have done and invalidates all of their worldly accomplishments. That is why, in another context,

God called it the House of Ruin (Dār al-Bawār)—meaning the House of Destruction: “Have you not regarded those who have changed Allah’s blessing with ingratitude, and landed their people in the house of ruin? Hell, which they shall enter, and it is an evil abode! (14:28–29). This illustrates the reality both phrases what they had accomplished in the world has failed and their works have come to naught are intended to explain: They are the ones for whom there shall be nothing in the Hereafter but Fire. There is nothing for them but the Fire, because everything else has been invalidated. From the above, it is clear that the meaning of recompensing them for their deeds in full means to actualize their results and convey the effects according to the system of cause and effect that governs the material and spiritual realms, not merely to deliver what the doer seeks by his action or hopes to attain by undertaking it. What the doer obtains in this life by his actions are the outcomes of these actions, which are determined by all the contributing factors, not merely what the doer conceives, no matter what it is, as not everything one desires is achievable.

God expressed this reality elsewhere, when He says, W hoever desires the tillage of the Hereafter, W e will enhance for him his tillage, and whoever desires the tillage of the world, We will give some of it to him, but he will have

no share in the Hereafter (42:20). Notice that He says, We will give some of it to him rather than ‘We will give it to him.’ In another verse, He says, W hoever desires this transitory life, W e expedite for him therein whatever We wish, for whomever We desire. Then We appoint hell for him, to enter it, blameful and spurned (17:18). In these verses, God says that the human being will obtain some of what He wishes for in this world but further clarifies that not everyone who desires a thing will necessarily attain it. On the contrary, the matter is up to God, who gives whatever He wills, withholds whatever He wills, and brings forward or holds back whomever He

wills according to the system of cause and effect that He has instituted in the universe.

Secondly, the two verses, by which I mean His saying: As for those who desire the life of this world and its glitter, W e will recompense them fully for their works therein… expound one of the divine realities.

Examining Narrations

(1) In al-Kāfī, regarding the verse, Look! They fold up their breasts …

(11:5), it is related from Ibn M aḥbūb, from Jāmīl b. Ṣāliḥ, from Sudayr, from Abū Jaʿfar, who said, ‘Jābir b. ʿAbd Allāh informed me that the idolaters, when they passed by the Messenger of God near the Kaʿba, one of them would lower his head and back in this manner, and cover his head with his robe so that the Prophet of God would not see him. Then God revealed, Look! They fold up their breasts …’

(2) In al-Durr al-M anthūr, al-Suyūṭī cites Ibn Abī Shaybah, Ibn alMundhir, Ibn Abū Ḥātim, and Abū al-Shaykh, who narrate from Abū Rizīn who said: ‘One of them would bend his back and cover himself with his garment.’

(3) In M ajmaʿ al-Bayān, al-Ṭabrisī reports from ʿAlī b. al-Ḥusayn and Abū Jaʿfar and Jaʿfar b. Muḥammad: ‘the verb “fold up”

(yathnūnī) is on the conjugation pattern of yafʿūʿal.’

(4) In Tafsīral-ʿAyyāshī, it is narrated from M uḥammad b. al-Fuḍayl, from Jābir, from Abū Jaʿfar who said: ‘A man from the Bedouins came to the Messenger of God and said: “O Messenger of God, I have sons and daughters, brothers and sisters, and grandsons and granddaughters, and the livelihood is light upon us. If you see fit, O Messenger of God, to ask God to increase it for us.”

Whereat the man began to weep, and the Muslims felt pity for him. The Prophet of God then said, “There is no animal on the earth, but that its sustenance lies with Allah, and He knows its abode and its temporary place of lodging. Everything is in a manifest Book. He who is responsible for putting food in these mouths, whose sustenance is guaranteed by God, God will pour sustenance upon him abundantly— like pouring water, if little then little, and if much then much.”’ The narrator added: ‘Then the Prophet of God prayed and the Muslims said “amen.”’

The narrator said, Abū Jaʿfar said: ‘I was then informed by someone who saw the man in the time of ʿUmar, and he asked him

about his situation, and he said: “Who is better than he who God made his income lawful and increased his wealth.”’

(5) In al-Durr al-M anthūr, al-Ḥakīm al-Tirmidhī reported in Nawādir al-Uṣūl, and al-Ḥākim al-Nīshābūrī authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī in Shuʿub al-Īmān, all narrate from Ibn Masʿūd, from the Prophet, who said: ‘When the

appointed term of one of you is in a particular land, a need for it is made available to him, until when he reaches his furthest step, he is seized by death, so the earth will say on the Day of Resurrection: ‘This is what was temporary lodged with me.”’

Author’s comment: The narration does not accord with the apparent meaning of the verse.

(6) In al-Kāfī, al-Kulaynī transmits via his chain of narrators from Abū Ḥamza al-Thumālī, from Abū Jaʿfar, who said: ‘The Messenger of God said during the Farewell Pilgrimage: “Behold, the Trustworthy Spirit has imparted to my mind that no soul will die until it completes its sustenance, so fear God and behave beautifully in its pursuit, and do not let delay of some of the sustenance

lead you to seek it by way of disobedience to God, for indeed God the Exalted has divided sustenance among His creation lawfully and has not divided them unlawfully. So, whoever fears God and is patient, his sustenance will come to him lawfully, and whoever tears the veil that God Almighty has drawn across it and seizes it unlawfully, his lawful sustenance will be reduced, and he will be held accountable for it.”’

Author’s comment: This tradition is well-known, narrated by both Sunnī and Shīʿī scholars via numerous chains of narration.

(7) In Tafsīr al-ʿAyyāshī, it is narrated from Abū al-Hadhīl, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh, who said: “Indeed God has divided all sustenance among His servants and has prepared a great grace that He has not divided among anyone. God has said: And ask Allah for His grace (4:32).’

Author’s comment: This tradition is also narrated from the Prophet and some reports in a similar vein has have already been presented in relation to His saying, and You provide for whomever You wish without any

reckoning (3:27), and His saying, And ask Allah for His grace (4:32). (8) In al-Kāfī, al-Kulaynī narrates from Abū ʿAbd Allāh, who said:

‘The Commander of the Faithful used to often say: “Know for certain that God Almighty has not made it possible for the servant— no matter how hard he strives, no matter how well he plans,

and no matter how abundant his schemes—to obtain what was assigned to him in the W ise Remembrance before its time. O people! A person will not increase in wealth by so much as a date thread through his cleverness, nor will a person decrease in wealth by so much as a date thread due to his stupidity. So, the one who realizes this and works according to it is the most relaxed of people in pursuing his own benefit, and the one who knows this but abandons it is the most dedicated of people in pursuing his own harm, and perhaps one who is blessed with kindness is gradually lured by kindness to Him and perhaps one who is conceited

among the people is led into perdition. So fear God, O you who strive, in your striving, and hold back from your haste, and wake up from your habitual heedlessness, and reflect on what has come from God Almighty upon the tongue of His Prophet.”’

(9) In al-Kāfī, al-Kulaynī relates via his chain of narrators from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Ḥajjāj, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh, who said: ‘Indeed, Muḥammad b. al-Munkadir used to say: “I did not think that ʿAlī b. Ḥusayn would leave behind a person better than him until I saw his son Muḥammad b. ʿAlī. I wanted to advise him, but he advised me.” His companions asked him:

“With what did he advise you?” He said: “I went out to some parts of Medina in a hot hour. I met Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad b. ʿAlī who was a bulky man, and he was leaning on two servant boys. I said to myself: ‘Glory be to God, one of the elders of the Quraysh is out at this hour, in such a state, in pursuit of this world! I will certainly advise him.’

I approached him and greeted him. He responded to me with difficulty while sweating heavily. I said: ‘May God rectify you, an elder of Quraysh out at this hour, in such a state, in pursuit of this world! What if your time came while you were in this state?’ He said: ‘If death came to me while I am in this state, it would have come to me while I am engaged in an act of obedience to God Almighty. It is through “this state” that I provide for myself and my dependents so that we do not need to rely on you or on other people, and I only fear that death would come to me while I am in a state of disobedience to God.’ So, I said: ‘You have spoken the truth, may God have mercy on you: I wanted to advise you, but it was you who advised me!’

(10) al-Kulaynī transmits via his chain of narrators, from ʿAbd al-Aʿlā, a freed slave of Āl Sām who said: ‘I met Abū ʿAbd Allāh in some roads of Medina on a hot summer’s day. I said: “May I be your ransom, even with your status with God Almighty and your closeness to the Messenger of God, you are exerting yourself on such a

day?” He said: “O ʿAbd al-Aʿlā, I went out in pursuit of sustenance, to be independent of seeking it from someone like you.”’ (ibid.)

Author’s comment: And there is no contradiction between the divine decree of apportioning sustenance to the creatures and the divine command to the creatures to seek it, as should be obvious.

(11) In al-Durr al-M anthūr, al-Ṭayālisī, Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal, al-Tirmidhī (who deemed it a good narration), Ibn Māja, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn alMundhir, Abū al-Shaykh in al-ʿAẓama, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Asmāʾ wa al-Ṣifāt all narrate from Abū Razīn who said: ‘I said: “O Messenger of God, where was our Lord before He created His creation?” He said: ‘He was in a cloud (ʿamāʾ), all that was below Him was air (mā taḥta-hu hawāʾ) and all that was above Him was air, and He created His throne over the water.”’

Author’s comment:ʿAmāʾ is a cloud that obscures one’s vision. When he says ‘all that was below Him was air and all that was above Him was air’, māʾ is a relative pronoun (mawṣūla). The meaning of hawāʾ is a void that is completely empty. This is the same as the meaning we observe in the verse, their hearts will be vacant (afʾidatu-hum hawāʾ) (14:43). Alternatively, we could read the māʾ as a negation (nāfiya) and hawāʾ as denoting the common meaning of ‘air.’ In this case, the tradition would mean that God was in a cloud that was not encompassed by air, unlike all other clouds. The narration is one of the traditions that, taken literally, seem to assign anthropomorphic qualities to God (tajassum), which is why when the Prophet says, ‘He was in a cloud’, this is to be understood as a metaphor for the unknowability of the Divine Essence, which confounds human intellects and bafiies perceptions.

(12) Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal, Bukhārī, Tirmidhī, Nasaʾī, Abū al-Shaykh in his book “al-ʿAẓama, Ibn Mardawayh, and Bayhaqī in al-Asmāʾ wa al-Ṣifāt all narrate from ʿImrān b. Ḥuṣayn, who said: ‘The people of Yemen asked: “O Messenger of God, tell us about the beginning of creation—how was it?” He replied: “God existed before everything, His throne was upon the water, He wrote the mention of everything in the Preserved Tablet, and created the heavens and the earth.” Then, a caller called out: “Your camel has gone astray, O son of Ḥuṣayn!” so he went away, and behold, it was a mirage that had deceived him. He said: “By God, I wish I had left it to roam.” (al-Durr al-Manthūr)

Author’s comment: Several scholars of traditions narrated this report from Burayda, and Burayda said at the end of it: ‘Then a man came to me and said: “Your camel has gone astray.” So I went out and it was a mirage that was deceiving him. I wish I had left it to roam.”’ This is a factor that weakens the two traditions.

(13) Concerning the verse, that He may test you: which of you is best in conduct (11:7), it is related from Dāwūd b. al-M uḥabbar in his book al-ʿAql, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim in al-Tārīkh, and Ibn Mardawayh, from Ibn ʿUmar who said: ‘The Messenger of God recited this verse: that He may test you: which of you is best in conduct, so I asked: “What does this mean, O Messenger of God?” He said: “It means to test which of you has the best intellect (ʿaql).” Then he said: “And the best of you in intellect is the most cautious of you concerning God’s prohibitions, and the most knowledgeable of you (or the most devoted of you) in obeying God”’ (ibid.)

(14) In al-Kāfī, al-Kulaynī narrates from Sufyān b. ʿUyayna, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh concerning the verse, that He may test you: which of you is best in conduct, he said: ‘This does not mean the one of you who performs the most actions, but the one who is most correct in his actions. Correctness is achieved through the fear of God and sincere intention.’

Then he said: ‘To persist in an action until it is purified is harder than the action itself, and the pure action is the one for which you do not wish to be praised by anyone except God Almighty.

The intention is better than the action. Indeed, the intention is the action!’ Then he recited the verse, Say, ‘Everyone acts according to his character …’ (17:84), meaning according to his intention.

Author’s comment: His statement, ‘Indeed, the intention is the action’, means that an action has no effect unless it is accompanied by the correct intention.

(15) In the Tafsīr of al-Nuʿmānī, it is transmitted via his chain of narration from Isḥāq b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh, regarding

the verse, if We defer their punishment until a certain time (umma maʿdūda) … (11:8), he said: ‘The punishment is the emergence of the Qāʾim, and the umma maʿdūda are the people of Badr and his Companions (where umma maʿdūda is understood in the sense of ‘numbered nation’ rather than ‘appointed time’).

Author’s comment:The same meaning is narrated by al-Kulaynī in al-Kāfī, and al-Qummī and al-ʿAyyāshī in their respective commentaries from ʿAlī, al-Bāqir, and al-Ṣādiq.

(16) In Majmaʿ al-Bayān, we read: ‘Some have said: “The numbered nation (umma maʿdūda) are the companions of the Mahdī— three hundred and a few more men, like the count of the people of Badr—they will gather together in an hour, as the autumn locusts gather.”’ Al-Ṭabrisī says: ‘And this is what is narrated from Abū Jaʿfar and Abū ʿAbd Allāh,.’

(17) In the Tafsīr of al-Qummī, regarding the verse, excepting those who are patient and do righteous deeds (11:11), we read: ‘He said:

“They are patient in adversity and continue to do good deeds in times of ease.”’

(18) In al-Durr al-M anthūr, regarding His saying, As for those who desire the life of this world … (11:15), al-Suyūṭī narrates from al-Bayhaqī, who narrated in Shuʿub al-Īmān from Anas, who said:

‘The Messenger of God, said: “When the Day of Resurrection comes, my community will be divided into three groups: a group who worshipped God purely, a group who worshipped God for show, and a group who worshipped God to achieve worldly gain.

He will say to the one who worshipped God for the world: ‘By My Majesty and Glory, what did you want with My worship?’ He will say: ‘The world.’ He will say: ‘Surely what you have gathered will not benefit you and you will not ever return to it—take him to the Fire!’ And He will say to the one who worshipped God for show: ‘By My Majesty and Glory, what did you want with My worship?’ He said: ‘To impress others.’ He will say: ‘Your worship with which you were showing of : nothing of it has ascended

to Me and nothing of it will benefit you today—take him to the Fire!’ And He will say to the one who worshipped God purely:

‘By My Majesty and Glory, what did you want with My worship?’

He will say: ‘By Your Majesty and Glory, for You know this better than I. I worshipped You for Your sake and for Your abode!’ He will say: ‘My servant has spoken the truth— take him to Paradise!’
